title: Jesus is no demon
source_text: Περιθεὶς δ᾿ ἡμῖν τοιούτους λόγους καὶ συκοφαντῶν Χριστιανοὺς, οὐ λέγοντας τὰ τοιαῦτα, ἑαυτῷ ἀπολογίαν πορίζειν νομίζει, παίγνιον μᾶλλον ἢ ἀπολογίαν τυγχάνουσαν, ἐν ᾗ φησιν ὡς πρὸς ἡμᾶς· οὐχ ὁρᾷς οὖν, ὦ βέλτιστε, ὅτι καὶ τὸν σὸν δαίμονα καταστάς τις οὐ βλασφημεῖ μόνον ἀλλὰ καὶ πάσης γῆς καὶ θαλάσσης ἐκκηρύττει καὶ σὲ τὸν καθωσιωμένον ὥσπερ ἄγαλμα αὐτῷ δήσας ἀπάγει καὶ ἀνασκολοπίζει· καὶ ὁ δαίμων ἢ, ὡς σὺ φῂς, ὁ τοῦ θεοῦ παῖς οὐδὲν αὐτὸν ἀμύνεται; χώραν δ᾿ εἶχεν ἡ ἀπολογία αὕτη, εἰ τοιούτοις λόγοις, ὁποίους ἡμᾶς ἀνέγραψε λέγοντας, ἐχρώμεθα· καίτοι γε οὐδ᾿ οὕτως ἀληθῆ ἔλεγε, δαίμονα εἰπὼν τὸν υἱὸν τοῦ θεοῦ. κατὰ μὲν οὖν ἡμᾶς, τοὺς λέγοντας πάντας δαίμονας εἶναι φαύλους, οὐ δαίμων ὁ τοὺς τοσούσδε ἐπιστρέψας πρὸς τὸν θεὸν ἀλλὰ θεὸς λόγος καὶ θεοῦ παῖς· κατὰ δὲ Κέλσον, μηδὲν ἐμφήναντα περὶ φαύλων δαιμόνων οὐκ οἶδ᾿ ὅπως ἐπιλαθόμενον ἑαυτοῦ, δαίμων ὁ Ἰησοῦς εἴρηται. ὕστερον μέντοι γε τὰ λεγόμενα περὶ τῶν ἀσεβῶν φθάσει μετὰ πάντα τὰ φάρμακα, ἅπερ οὐ προσήκαντο, ἐπὶ τοὺς καταλαμβανομένους ἐν τῇ, ὡς ἂν εἴποι τις, ἀνιάτῳ κακίᾳ.
pass_a_gloss: Having put around (περιτίθημι) us such words and slandering (συκοφαντέω) Christians, who do not say such things, he thinks (νομίζω) to provide (πορίζω) himself a defence (ἀπολογία), being rather a jest (παίγνιον) than a defence, in which he says as to us: 'do you not see then, my best fellow (ὦ βέλτιστε), that someone, having taken a stand (καθίστημι), not only blasphemes (βλασφημέω) your demon (δαίμων) but also proclaims him banished (ἐκκηρύττω) from every land and sea, and binding (δέω) you, the one consecrated (καθοσιόω) to him like a statue (ἄγαλμα), leads away (ἀπάγω) and impales (ἀνασκολοπίζω); and the demon or, as you say, the child of God (ὁ τοῦ θεοῦ παῖς) does not at all avenge himself on (ἀμύνομαι) him?' This defence would have had place (χώρα) if we used such words as he recorded (ἀναγράφω) us saying; and yet not even so would he say true things, calling the Son (υἱός) of God a demon. According to us, then, who say all demons are base (φαῦλος), the one who turned (ἐπιστρέφω) so many toward God is not a demon but God Word (θεὸς λόγος) and child of God; but according to Celsus, having shown (ἐμφαίνω) nothing about base demons, forgetting himself I know not how, Jesus has been called a demon. Later (ὕστερον) however the things said about the impious (ἀσεβής) will overtake (φθάνω), after all the remedies (φάρμακα) which they did not admit (προσίεμαι), those caught (καταλαμβάνω) in the, as one might say, incurable (ἀνίατος) wickedness (κακία).
pass_b_english: Having put such words in our mouths and slandered Christians, who say no such things, he thinks he is furnishing himself with a defence, though it is a jest rather than a defence. In it he says, as if to us: “Do you not see, my good man, that someone takes his stand and not only blasphemes even your demon, but has him banished by proclamation from every land and sea, and binds you, who are consecrated to him like a statue, leads you away and impales you; and the demon, or, as you say, the Son of God, takes no vengeance on him?”

This defence would have had some place if we used such words as he has written down that we say; and yet even then he would not have spoken the truth in calling the Son of God a demon. In our view, since we say that all demons are wicked, the One who turned so many people to God is not a demon but God the Word and Son of God. But according to Celsus, who has made nothing plain about wicked demons and has forgotten himself, how I do not know, Jesus is called a demon.
Later, however, after all the remedies that they did not accept, what is said about the ungodly will come upon those who are found in what one might call incurable wickedness.

choices.choice: Celsus uses παῖς (‘child’) for the Son of God, and Origen echoes it in θεοῦ παῖς; rendered ‘Son of God’ in both places for natural English, with υἱός also ‘Son’. ἐκκηρύττει rendered ‘has him banished by proclamation’; ἀνασκολοπίζει ‘impales’ (the word Celsus uses for crucifixion of Christians). θεὸς λόγος rendered ‘God the Word’ (compare John 1:1, not a quotation, so not cited inline). The sentence about Celsus is compressed in the Greek: Celsus elsewhere has not said demons are wicked, yet here calls Jesus a demon, which Origen treats as self-contradiction (‘forgetting himself’). ‘The things spoken about the ungodly’ refers generally to Scripture’s warnings of punishment; no single verse identified.
Celsus's words: 'someone stands up even against your demon' -> 'someone takes his stand and not only blasphemes even your demon' (καταστάς has no 'against'; καί on the demon)
'like an image' -> 'like a statue' (ἄγαλμα, consistent with 8.38)

'in Celsus's account, though he has ... and has somehow forgotten himself' -> 'according to Celsus, who has ... and has forgotten himself, how I do not know' (οὐκ οἶδ᾿ ὅπως kept in Origen's voice; no added concession)
last sentence reordered to natural English; 'would not accept' -> 'did not accept' (aorist, no modality); 'overtake' -> 'come upon' (φθάνω ἐπί)

choices.choice: 8.39 keeps 'Son of God' for both Celsus's ὁ τοῦ θεοῦ παῖς and Origen's θεοῦ παῖς, as the translator's note says. This is defensible but loses Celsus's 'child'. The owner could choose 'child of God' as house style.
